addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - API usage, tool use, Anthropic SDK usage. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## npx
NotebookLM MCP - Access NotebookLM (notebooklm.google.com).

**Auth:** If you get authentication errors, run `nlm login` via your Bash/terminal tool. This is the automated authentication method that handles everything. Only use save_auth_tokens as a fallback if the CLI fails.
**Account Switching:** To switch Google Accounts for the MCP server, run `nlm login switch <profile>` in Bash. The MCP server instantly uses the active default profile.
**Confirmation:** Tools with confirm param require user approval before setting confirm=True.
**Studio:** After creating audio/video/infographic/slides, poll studio_status for completion.

Consolidated tools:
- source_add(source_type=url|text|drive|file, url=..., document_id=..., text=..., file_path=...): Add any source type
- studio_create(artifact_type=audio|video|...): Create any artifact type
- studio_revise: Revise individual slides in an existing slide deck
- download_artifact(artifact_type=audio|video|...): Download any artifact type
- note_create/note_list/note_update/note_delete: Manage notes in notebooks

attachment.content:
- skills: Reference codebase for Crates. Use this skill when you need to understand the structure, implementation patterns, or code details of the Crates project.
- mcp-server-dev:build-mcp-app: This skill should be used when the user wants to build an "MCP app", add "interactive UI" or "widgets" to an MCP server, "render components in chat", build "MCP UI resources", make a tool that shows a "form", "picker", "dashboard" or "confirmation dialog" inline in the conversation, or mentions "apps SDK" in the context of MCP. Use AFTER the build-mcp-server skill has settled the deployment model, or when the user already knows they want UI widgets.
- mcp-server-dev:build-mcp-server: This skill should be used when the user asks to "build an MCP server", "create an MCP", "make an MCP integration", "wrap an API for Claude", "expose tools to Claude", "make an MCP app", or discusses building something with the Model Context Protocol. It is the entry point for MCP server development — it interrogates the user about their use case, determines the right deployment model (remote HTTP, MCPB, local stdio), picks a tool-design pattern, and hands off to specialized skills.
- mcp-server-dev:build-mcpb: This skill should be used when the user wants to "package an MCP server", "bundle an MCP", "make an MCPB", "ship a local MCP server", "distribute a local MCP", discusses ".mcpb files", mentions bundling a Node or Python runtime with their MCP server, or needs an MCP server that interacts with the local filesystem, desktop apps, or OS and must be installable without the user having Node/Python set up.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

content.text: I'll sweep the system logs for errors and warnings. Since this is Artix (s6-rc, not systemd), I'll check dmesg, s6 logs, and traditional log files rather than journalctl.

input.description: Check dmesg for errors and warnings

<!DOCTYPE busconfig PUBLIC
 "-//freedesktop//DTD D-BUS Bus Configuration 1.0//EN"
 "http://www.freedesktop.org/standards/dbus/1.0/busconfig.dtd">
<busconfig>
  <!-- 
    D-Bus policy for op-dbus Agent Services
    
    Agents register as: org.dbusmcp.Agent.{AgentType}
    Example: org.dbusmcp.Agent.RustPro
    
    The ChatActor discovers these via introspection and
    creates tools that call the Execute method.
  -->

  <!-- Allow root to own agent services -->
  <policy user="root">
    <allow own_prefix="org.dbusmcp"/>
    <allow send_destination_prefix="org.dbusmcp"/>
    <allow receive_sender_prefix="org.dbusmcp"/>
  </policy>

  <!-- Allow op-dbus user to own and call -->
  <policy user="op-dbus">
    <allow own_prefix="org.dbusmcp"/>
    <allow send_destination_prefix="org.dbusmcp"/>
    <allow receive_sender_prefix="org.dbusmcp"/>
  </policy>

  <!-- Allow any user to call agent methods (for chat interface) -->
  <policy context="default">
    <!-- Agent interface -->
    <allow send_destination_prefix="org.dbusmcp.Agent"
           send_interface="org.dbusmcp.Agent"/>
    
    <!-- Standard D-Bus introspection -->
    <allow send_destination_prefix="org.dbusmcp"
           send_interface="org.freedesktop.DBus.Introspectable"/>
    <allow send_destination_prefix="org.dbusmcp"
           send_interface="org.freedesktop.DBus.Properties"/>
    <allow send_destination_prefix="org.dbusmcp"
           send_interface="org.freedesktop.DBus.Peer"/>
  </policy>
</busconfig>

Now I can answer both points precisely.

## Where `10.220.x.x` came from

It's the **netmaker mesh interface** — and it's the wrong place to point anything right now:

```
netmaker   DOWN   10.220.35.1/24  fd42:464d:b07:32b8::1/64
ovsbr0     UP     10.200.0.1/30
```

`10.220.35.1/24` is assigned to the `netmaker` interface, which is **DOWN**. I surfaced that address from two stale sources — the earlier `ss` output (a DNS listener still bound to that now-down iface) and my stored memory note `project_cognitive_grpc_endpoint.md` ("live cognitive-mcp gRPC is 10.220.35.1:50052"). That memory even flags itself as having a stale variant. On *this* running box, `op-cognitive-mcp` actually listens on `0.0.0.0:50052`, not on the netmaker address. So `10.220.35.1` was never a real target for `assistant` — that was my mistake for pulling it into the recommendation. Good catch.

## You're right — assistant should be a socket, not an IP

That's the real architectural smell. Right now the assistant gRPC is a **TCP** listener:

```
LISTEN  10.200.0.1:50051   op-dbus (pid 3261)
```

…and `zeroclaw-gui-srv/run` reaches it as `ZEROCLAW_GRPC=http://assistant.3tched.com:50051` — a hostname→IP→TCP path. That contradicts the socket-first design (Unix domain sockets + the shared `ovsbr0-sock`, xray identity-routed). The only `assistant` socket currently present is the Incus command socket (`@/var/lib/incus/containers/assistant/command`), not a gRPC one.

So the fix direction isn't "pin the hostname to an IP" — it's "stop using a hostname/TCP endpoint at all and point zeroclaw at a UDS." Let me confirm what socket the assistant gRPC should expose:

**HARD RULE: no container is to have a NIC or an IP.** Containers reach the host and each other ONLY over Unix domain sockets — disk/socket passthrough devices (e.g. `assistant`'s `host-op-dbus-session` mount of `/run/op-dbus/session-bus.sock`) or the shared `ovsbr0-sock` (see [[project_socket_provisioning]]), identity-routed by xray (see [[project_identity_injection]], [[project_zero_trust_principle]]). Verified 2026-06-21: every container shows empty IPV4 and `assistant` has no `eth*`/`nic`/`proxy` device — only `*-overlay`, `host-op-dbus-session`, `root`.

**Why:** matches the SHM-reactive, socket-first design — arrival over a socket triggers action, no NIC means no listening IP surface to ACL/firewall (theater). gRPC **reflection works directly over a UDS** — that is how it "worked directly" historically; it does NOT need a TCP host:port.

**How to apply:** NEVER point a client at a container via `http://host:port` or a hostname like `assistant.3tched.com:50051`. The assistant gRPC must be reached over a socket. `10.200.0.1` (ovsbr0) and `10.220.35.1` (netmaker, usually DOWN) are HOST bridge addresses — do not treat them as container endpoints or "fix" anything by pinning a name to them. The regression to watch for: services configured with `ZEROCLAW_GRPC=http://assistant.3tched.com:50051` / `OP_ASSISTANT_RPC_ENDPOINT=http://10.200.0.1:50051` — those TCP paths violate this rule and should move to UDS. Corrects/supersedes the IP framing in [[project_cognitive_grpc_endpoint]].

content.text:
Now I have the whole story — and the answer to your "even Lovable had it working" question. **Lovable *is* the zeroclaw-gui client**, and it only ever spoke TCP. Here's the timeline and the actual cause:

## No container got an IP

Verified again: every container has empty IPV4, `assistant` has no NIC. The only container that ever carries an IP is `wg-xray` (`10.200.0.2`, the far end of the ovsbr0 `/30` point-to-point) — and it's **STOPPED**. The `10.200.0.x` / `10.220.x` addresses are **host** bridge interfaces, not containers.

## What actually changed (when + how)

The zeroclaw-gui binary is built from **`lovable/.zeroclaw/`** — that's Lovable. Its client is hard-wired to TCP gRPC, by its own UI text:

```
lovable/.zeroclaw/src/main.rs:23          let endpoint = std::env::var("ZEROCLAW_GRPC")
lovable/.zeroclaw/src/views/mod.rs:229    "Set ZEROCLAW_GRPC=http://host:port and restart.
                                           Server must register tonic_reflection..."
```

It has **no Unix-socket transport** — only `http://host:port`. So when it "worked directly with reflection/gRPC a couple hours ago," it was dialing a reachable **TCP** endpoint (the grpc-bridge that used to answer on `10.200.0.x:50051`).

Today, two things landed (commits `971ee905 zeroclaw` + `f530c7c4 "zeroclaw Axum host and remaining runtime wiring"`, and `zeroclaw-gui-srv/run` was rewritten at **12:51**):

1. The bridge's intended transport moved to a **host UDS** `/run/opdbus/zeroclaw-grpc.sock` (`server.rs:35/220`) — the right direction for "no container IP."
2. But `zeroclaw-gui-srv/run` was given `ZEROCLAW_GRPC=http://assistant.3tched.com:50051` — a TCP **hostname** that doesn't resolve — and the UDS-serving bridge **isn't running** (only the older op-dbus TCP `:50051` is).

So nothing gave a container an IP. The reflection break is a **client/transport mismatch introduced at 12:51 today**: the Lovable GUI can only do TCP, but it was pointed at an unresolvable name while the bridge was being moved to a socket it can't dial.

## The real tension to resolve

Your rule (no container NIC/IP, everything UDS) collides with Lovable's TCP-only client. Two ways out:

- **Host-loopback TCP** — serve reflection on `127.0.0.1:50051` on the *host* and set `ZEROCLAW_GRPC=http://127.0.0.1:50051`. Honors the rule (host loopback isn't a container NIC) and Lovable works unmodified. Lowest friction.
- **Teach Lovable UDS** — add a `unix:` connector to `lovable/.zeroclaw/src/main.rs` (tonic `connect_with_connector` over `UnixStream`) so it dials `/run/opdbus/zeroclaw-grpc.sock` directly. Architecturally pure, but a code change to the Lovable client.

Which direction do you want? If host-loopback, I can point `zeroclaw-gui-srv/run` at `127.0.0.1:50051` now and confirm the bridge answers reflection there.

content.text:
Definitive answer: **op-projection.** Here's the proof, not a guess:

## op-projection is the current one

`SystemPluginReader::new()` (plugin_reader.rs:58-62) does:
```rust
let registry = DefaultPluginRegistry::new(state_store);
let plugins = registry.load_all_plugins().await?;   // loads ALL plugins directly
```
It loads every plugin straight from the registry, resolves each one's **schemars** schema, and serves them as readable objects at **`/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<plugin>`** (`org.opdbus.v1.plugins.ProjectedObject`) on the **system bus**. That *is* your design — direct plugin lookup, schema-is-the-plugin, readable named fields. No snapshot, no aggregate.

## op-dbus-mirror is legacy — and it's the thing that confused us

- op-projection → owns `org.opdbus.v1.plugins` on the **system bus** (pid 3270) ← the real readable tree
- op-dbus-mirror → owns the same name on the **session bus** (pid 3273) ← the empty `PluginsV1` snapshot

Every introspection I did earlier hit the **session bus**, so I kept landing on op-dbus-mirror's dead snapshot (`as 0`). That's why it looked like "the tree broke." The tree didn't break — **we were reading the retired service.**

## The catch

op-projection owns the system-bus name but introspection **times out with zero objects** — it's up but not mounting the tree (wedged or fell back to `empty()` during `load_all_plugins`/state query). So neither path is actually serving right now: mirror serves empty, projection serves nothing.

## So the real shape of the fix (totally different from where I started)

1. **Retire op-dbus-mirror** as the plugin-tree publisher — it shouldn't be co-owning `org.opdbus.v1.plugins` (on any bus). That alone kills the snapshot/`PluginsV1` confusion.
2. **Fix op-projection** so it actually mounts `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<plugin>` from `load_all_plugins` — that restores the readable named-field tree.
3. The **bridge** is a separate consumer that reads the SHM file `/dev/shm/opdbus/schemas/zeroclaw.json` — that write path still needs an owner (it's currently orphaned inside the dead snapshot trigger).

Before I touch anything: do you want me to dig into **why op-projection serves an empty tree** (is `load_all_plugins` erroring, or is it mounting then the query hangs)? That's the thing to fix — op-dbus-mirror can just be stopped.

content.text:
Real tradeoffs, grounded in how *this* system uses it — not a generic answer:

## What a separate-folder approach buys you
- **Write isolation** — each plugin is the sole writer of its own `<plugin>.json`, no read-modify-write of a 575KB monolith, no torn reads when one plugin updates. (The zeroclaw doc comment literally assumed this: "the plugin is the sole writer of `…/schemas/zeroclaw.json`.")
- **Granular reload** — SIGHUP/mutation for one plugin touches one file; a watcher could reload just that entry instead of re-parsing the whole catalog.
- **Smaller targeted reads** — a consumer that only wants zeroclaw reads ~5KB, not 575KB.
- **`ls` = the plugin list** — the folder *is* the enumerator, which is conceptually clean and matches "the schema is the plugin."

## What the monolith buys you — and why it wins *here*
The decisive one is specific to your current branch (`feat/sled-source-port-salt`):

```
schema_bridge.rs:795  Blake3( wg_pubkey || schema_catalog_hash(/dev/shm/live-schema.json)
                              || mutation_index || source_port )
```

**The whole `live-schema.json` is hashed as `schema_catalog_hash` — it's a cryptographic identity primitive**, not just data. A single file gives **one deterministic hash over a consistent snapshot of all 63 plugins**. Split it into a folder and you now have to define a canonical hash across N files (ordering, concatenation, merkle) — fragile, and you can observe the folder mid-update (some files new, some old) → an ambiguous catalog hash → auth derivation races. Plus the monolith gives **atomic catalog swaps** (one `rename`) and there are already **9+ readers** (`op-identity`, `op-web` ×4, `op-projection`, `op-cognitive-mcp`, `op-grpc-bridge`, `factory`, `unix_socket`) all pointed at the one path.

## My honest read
For this codebase, **keep the monolith.** The folder's benefits (write isolation, granular reload) are real but mostly matter at high plugin-update frequency — and you'd be trading them against breaking/complicating the schema-catalog-hash identity derivation and the atomic-snapshot guarantee, which are load-bearing.

If you ever *do* want per-plugin write isolation, the non-destructive shape is a **hybrid**: plugins own per-plugin files in a folder, and the enumerator rolls them into `live-schema.json` (the canonical, hashed, atomically-swapped catalog) — folder for writes, monolith for the hash + readers. But that's a system-wide change, and for zeroclaw specifically (new, unimportant, your words) it's not worth it — just point it at `live-schema.json` like everything else.

content.text:
You're right — I overstated that. Yes, you can absolutely derive a deterministic catalog hash from a folder; it's a standard pattern (it's basically what git trees and Nix do). My "monolith wins because of the hash" framing was too strong.

## How you'd hash the folder (deterministically)
```
catalog_hash = blake3(
    for each plugin_id in sorted(folder):       # canonical order
        plugin_id || blake3(canonical_bytes(file))
)
```
Sort the entries, hash `(name, content)` pairs, fold them — a Merkle-style digest. Same strength and determinism as hashing the monolith, as long as you pin three things: **canonical ordering** (sorted ids), **canonical encoding** (raw bytes, or canonicalized JSON — pick one), and **what's included** (ignore temp/dotfiles). So the hash is *not* a reason to avoid the folder.

## The real remaining concerns (smaller than I implied, and solvable)
1. **Both ends must agree on the algorithm.** The catalog hash isn't computed in one place — `op-identity` uses it in ~4 spots (`schema_bridge.rs`, `anna_scribe.rs`, `op-sled-top.rs`, `op-identity-sled.rs`), and whatever verifies on the *other* side of the WG/ghostbridge derivation must compute the **identical** folder-hash. With a monolith it's trivially "blake3 these bytes." With a folder, every party must implement the exact same canonical fold. That's the actual friction — interop, not feasibility.
2. **Atomic snapshot during concurrent writes.** Hashing N files while a writer updates one mid-scan gives a torn catalog. Solvable: write to a temp dir and `rename()` the directory, or have the enumerator drop a tiny **manifest** (`index.json` with the precomputed `catalog_hash` + per-file hashes) atomically — readers/verifiers trust the manifest, writers own individual files.

## So the clean design you're pointing at
Folder of per-plugin schemas = **source of truth** (write isolation, `ls` = plugin list), plus an atomically-written **manifest** carrying the canonical hash. Then:
- the hash derivation reads the manifest (one atomic read, deterministic),
- consumers read individual files,
- the monolithic `live-schema.json` either goes away or becomes a *derived cache* of the folder.

That gets you the per-plugin benefits **and** the identity hash, with no torn-snapshot problem. The only real work is making both sides of the auth derivation compute the manifest hash identically — that's the thing to get right, not the hashing itself.

content.text: Let me look at what `gemma.rs` actually does before judging whether it should exist — that's the only way to answer it honestly:

Good instinct — and looking at it, you're basically right: **`gemma.rs` isn't Gemma.** It's not inference and it's not routing. It's a thin REST shim for the lovable SPA's UI-spec gallery. Four handlers:

| Endpoint | What it does |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/gemma/specs` | reads `/dev/shm/gemma-ui-specs.json`, returns it |
| `DELETE /api/gemma/specs/:id` | removes one spec from that JSON, atomic rewrite |
| `POST /api/gemma/regenerate` | **shells out** to the `/usr/local/bin/op-gemma` binary |
| `GET /api/gemma/catalog` | passthrough-reads `/dev/shm/live-schema.json` |

So the actual Gemma work is exactly where you said — the **`op-gemma` binary** (which is what talks to Ollama), plus the routing/subid-classification that lives in the xray/plugin stack. This file is just CRUD over a `/dev/shm` artifact + a "run the binary" button.

And by your own architecture, it **shouldn't be a bespoke `.rs` handler:**

1. **The `regenerate` handler `tokio::process::Command::new("/usr/local/bin/op-gemma")`** — spawning a subprocess straight from the web tier. That bypasses the mutation engine / "every mutation is an enforcement point." A regenerate should be a **plugin mutation / D-Bus method**, not a fork from op-web.
2. **`specs` and `catalog` are generic SHM-JSON passthroughs** — not Gemma-specific logic. The gallery (`gemma-ui-specs.json`) is just another `/dev/shm` artifact that should be served as a **projection** under `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins`, like everything else — not a hand-written endpoint.

So the clean shape matches your hunch: **a Gemma plugin** that owns spec generation + routing, exposes `regenerate` as a mutation, and publishes the gallery as a projection — and op-web serves it generically. The bespoke `gemma.rs` handler is the kind of one-off surface that the schema/plugin/projection design exists to eliminate.

Footnote on the build: this file is *also* the thing breaking the op-dbus compile — line 36 is malformed (`Path(spec_id: String) -> Path<String>)` should be `Path(spec_id): Path<String>`), and `spec_id` is undefined downstream as a result. It's half-finished WIP. If it's going to become a plugin anyway, that's a reason not to bother repairing the handler as-is — delete it and route Gemma through a plugin instead.

Want me to (a) just unbreak the syntax so op-dbus builds now, or (b) leave it since it's headed for the plugin treatment? Your call.

Recorded. Here's the concrete mapping — what the plugin absorbs:

| `gemma.rs` today | GemmaPlugin equivalent |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/gemma/specs` (read gallery JSON) | `query_current_state` → gallery published as projection under `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/gemma` |
| `DELETE /api/gemma/specs/:id` | a **mutation** (remove spec) routed through MutationEngine → Event Chain audit + policy |
| `POST /api/gemma/regenerate` (forks `op-gemma`) | a **mutation** that triggers generation — no `Command::new` from the web tier |
| `GET /api/gemma/catalog` (reads live-schema) | already generic — it's just the catalog everyone reads; no Gemma-specific handler needed |
| schema/config | schemars struct w/ OSCAL subids: model, Ollama endpoint, the 4 perspectives |

Inference stays where it belongs — `op-gemma` → Ollama. The plugin is the **control/state/routing** surface; the model lives in Ollama. Registered in `default_registry.rs`, served generically like every other plugin, and `handlers/gemma.rs` + the `/api/gemma/*` routes get deleted.

There's a nice convergence here: **deleting `gemma.rs` is both the first step toward the plugin *and* the thing that unblocks the op-dbus build** (it's the file with the syntax error). So you don't have to choose between "fix the build" and "do it right" — removing the handler does both, and op-dbus rebuilds clean so the `MutationEngine` rename can deploy.

So the sequence I'd suggest:
1. **Delete `handlers/gemma.rs` + its route registrations** → op-dbus builds → rename deploys. (small, unblocks everything)
2. **Scaffold `GemmaPlugin`** (schemars struct + `StatePlugin` impl + registry entry) as its own piece of work.

Want me to do **#1** now (delete the handler + unwire the routes, confirm op-web compiles)? That's contained and gets you a building tree again. #2 is the bigger build — I'd start it as a separate focused pass once you're ready.

content.text:
That's the right cut — you're separating **the model** from **what Gemma *does*.** Two distinct plugins:

## 1. `large-language-model` (generic, model-agnostic)
The inference surface. The model is just a **field**, not the identity:
- config (schemars): `provider` (ollama), `model_id` (gemma3 / llama / mistral…), endpoint, generation params, maybe pull/load lifecycle
- this is the *only* thing that knows about Ollama. Swap the model by changing a value — matches your "broker/model is swappable" stance.
- "Gemma the model" becomes `model_id: "gemma3"` here. Nothing else hard-codes Gemma.

## 2. The Gemma **role** plugin (the brain, not the model)
The consumer that does the *work*, delegating inference to the LLM plugin:
- **tag routing + subid classification** (your "Gemma owns subid classification AND tag routing")
- the **4 perspectives** (Data/Numeric, Spatial/Layout, User Flow, Context/Aesthetic)
- UI-spec generation (what `gemma.rs` was shimming)
- it *calls* `large-language-model`; it doesn't embed a model.

So the boundary is clean: **LLM plugin = *how* to talk to a model. Gemma plugin = *what to decide* with it.**

## On the name (your three)
Since the model is now generic, the role plugin should be named for its **function**, and that's exactly what your options do. My read of the scope:

- **`gemma-router`** — crispest, matches its headline job (xray tag routing + subid classification). Best if routing *is* the job.
- **`gemma-brain`** — umbrella term; fits if it's a multi-function decision unit (routing **+** classification **+** UI perspectives all under one roof).
- **`gemma-logic`** — vaguest; I'd drop it.

I'd lean **`gemma-router`** if you want single-responsibility plugins (routing one concern, UI-gen possibly its own later), or **`gemma-brain`** if it's deliberately the one cognitive plugin that owns all the Gemma decisions.

One honest flag: if the model is truly swappable, "gemma" in the *role* name is a brand, not a binding — the brain could run on any model. That's fine if "Gemma" is your name for the brain concept; just know it's branding, not coupling.

Which way — `gemma-router` (single-purpose) or `gemma-brain` (umbrella)? And is `large-language-model` the name you want for the generic one, or shorter like `llm`?

**Decision (2026-06-21): Gemma becomes a `StatePlugin`, not an op-web handler.** The existing `crates/op-web/src/handlers/gemma.rs` is a bespoke REST shim (4 handlers: read `/dev/shm/gemma-ui-specs.json`, delete a spec, `POST regenerate` that **forks `/usr/local/bin/op-gemma`**, passthrough `/dev/shm/live-schema.json`). That is exactly the surface the schema/plugin/projection design exists to eliminate. (It's also broken WIP — `gemma.rs:36` `Path(spec_id: String) -> Path<String>)` is malformed, blocking the op-dbus build.)

**The general anti-pattern:** an op-web handler that (a) bespoke-reads a `/dev/shm` artifact or (b) forks a binary is wrong. State → a plugin's `query_current_state` published as a **projection** under `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<plugin>` (read generically, not via `/api/gemma/*`). Actions → **mutations routed through the MutationEngine** (op-grpc-bridge) so they hit the Event Chain audit + policy enforcement ("every mutation is an enforcement point"); never `tokio::process::Command` from the web tier.

**GemmaPlugin shape:** schemars-derived typed struct(s) with OSCAL subids (config: model, Ollama endpoint, the 4 perspectives — see [[project_gemma_4perspectives]]); owns the UI-spec gallery as state/projection; `regenerate`/`delete-spec` as mutations; Gemma routing/subid-classification lives here (see [[project_subid_taxonomy]], [[project_xray_router]]). Inference itself stays in the `op-gemma` binary → Ollama (plugin orchestrates, model stays in Ollama). Register in `op-plugins/src/default_registry.rs`. Then DELETE `handlers/gemma.rs` + its `/api/gemma/*` routes. Honors [[project_one_schema_single_source]].

input.new_string:
**Two-plugin split (named 2026-06-21):**
- **`large-language-model`** — generic, model-AGNOSTIC inference surface. schemars config: `provider` (ollama), `model_id` (gemma3/llama/mistral…), endpoint, gen params, pull/load lifecycle. The ONLY thing that knows about Ollama. "Gemma the model" = `model_id: "gemma3"` here; nothing else hard-codes Gemma. Swappable broker stance.
- **`gemma-brain`** — umbrella COGNITIVE plugin (Gemma does multiple things, so "brain" not "router"). Owns: tag routing + subid classification (see [[project_subid_taxonomy]], [[project_xray_router]]), the 4 perspectives (see [[project_gemma_4perspectives]]), UI-spec gallery generation. CONSUMES `large-language-model` for inference — does not embed a model. "gemma" here is a brand for the brain concept, not a model binding.

Boundary: **LLM plugin = HOW to talk to a model; gemma-brain = WHAT to decide with it.** Both schemars-derived with OSCAL subids; state→projection under `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<plugin>`; actions (`regenerate`/`delete-spec`)→mutations via MutationEngine. Register in `op-plugins/src/default_registry.rs`. Then DELETE `handlers/gemma.rs` + its `/api/gemma/*` routes (also unblocks the op-dbus build). Honors [[project_one_schema_single_source]].

content.text:
Locked in and recorded. The settled design:

- **`large-language-model`** — generic, model-agnostic. Model is a field (`model_id: "gemma3"`). The only thing that touches Ollama. Swap models without touching anything else.
- **`gemma-brain`** — umbrella cognitive plugin (multiple jobs → "brain," not "router"): tag routing, subid classification, the 4 perspectives, UI-spec generation. Consumes `large-language-model`; embeds no model.
- Boundary: **LLM plugin = *how* to talk to a model; `gemma-brain` = *what to decide* with it.**

Proposed build sequence:

1. **Delete `handlers/gemma.rs` + unwire `/api/gemma/*` routes** — contained, and it unblocks the op-dbus build so the `MutationEngine` rename can deploy. (small)
2. **Scaffold `large-language-model`** — schemars config struct (provider/model_id/endpoint/params) + `StatePlugin` impl + registry entry. The Ollama-facing surface. (medium)
3. **Scaffold `gemma-brain`** — schemars struct for its config + state; `StatePlugin` impl; `regenerate`/`delete-spec` as mutations; gallery as projection; delegates inference to `large-language-model`. (the big one)

We've made a lot of decisions this session — the `MutationEngine` rename is done (just needs the build unblocked to deploy), and the Gemma direction is now fully specified and saved.

Want me to do **#1 now** (delete the handler, unwire the routes, confirm op-web compiles, so the rename can build/deploy)? That's the clean, low-risk step that gets you a building tree. #2 and #3 are real implementation passes I'd take one at a time when you're ready to build them out.

If the gallery is **live**, then deleting `gemma.rs` doesn't just unblock the build, it **takes down the running UI** — the lovable SPA polls `/api/gemma/specs`, `/regenerate`, `/specs/:id`, and `op-gemma` is already producing the 200 specs into `/dev/shm/gemma-ui-specs.json`. So I should *not* delete it yet.

Reframing with that in mind:

- **UI-gen stays exactly as-is.** The engine is the `op-gemma` binary (→ Ollama, the 4 perspectives). That's working and the plugin migration **must not reimplement it** — `gemma-brain` will *orchestrate* the same binary/artifact, not replace the generation.
- **What migrates is only the *surface*:** bespoke `/api/gemma/*` handlers → `gemma-brain` publishing the gallery as a **projection** and exposing `regenerate`/`delete-spec` as **mutations**. That's a clean cutover you do *when the projection is ready* — not before, or the gallery goes dark.

So the corrected sequence:

1. **Minimal fix now** — just repair the one-line syntax error so op-web builds and the gallery keeps working:
   ```
   gemma.rs:36   Path(spec_id: String) -> Path<String>)   →   Path(spec_id): Path<String>
   ```
   That fixes both the syntax error and the three `spec_id`-not-in-scope errors (it's the same root cause), unblocks the op-dbus build → `MutationEngine` rename deploys, **and the live UI-gen gallery stays up.**
2. **Build `large-language-model` + `gemma-brain`** as before — `gemma-brain` wraps the existing UI-gen (and adds routing/classification).
3. **Cut over** — once `gemma-brain` serves the gallery as a projection + mutations, *then* delete `gemma.rs` and the `/api/gemma/*` routes. No gap.

So I had it backwards on deletion — keeping a working feature alive wins. Want me to apply the **one-line syntax fix** now (unblocks the build, preserves the gallery), and leave the handler in place until `gemma-brain` is ready to take over?

content.text:
Honestly? **The *direction* is nailed down; the *implementation and a few concrete specifics* are not.** Let me separate them cleanly so it's not fuzzy:

## ✅ Decided (and the rename is even coded)
- **Two engines, distinct names:** `SchemaEngine` (op-projection) = schema/catalog authority; `MutationEngine` (op-grpc-bridge) = mutation authority. They map to the two hash terms. *(rename implemented + compiles)*
- **One enumerator:** `op-projection::SchemaEngine::write_schemas_to_shm()` is the single producer of the catalog. No competing writer.
- **Dual SHM view from one producer:** folder of per-plugin files (`…/schemas/<plugin>.json`, individual consumption) **+** loose `live-schema.json` (collective / derived cache). Same pass, can't diverge.
- **Hash strategy:** per-plugin **leaf** hashes + one folded **root** (incremental — a schema change re-hashes only that plugin), in **one** `schema_catalog_hash()` function. Monolith stops being the hash source.

## ❗ Not yet nailed (decisions to make before building)
1. **Individual-file format** — is `…/schemas/zeroclaw.json` the bare `PluginSchema` object, or the `[schema]` array like the monolith's value? (The zeroclaw bridge currently expects the bare object.) Pick one shape for all per-plugin files.
2. **How `op-identity` *obtains* the single hash** — does it read a small **manifest** (`/dev/shm/opdbus/schemas/index.json` carrying the root hash), call a function, or read a SHM value? Right now it re-reads + re-hashes in **5 places** — that consolidation isn't designed yet, just agreed in principle.
3. **Atomic update mechanism** — per-file temp+rename, or atomic dir swap, or manifest-gated. Agreed it must be atomic; the *how* isn't chosen.

## 🔲 Not built at all
- The folder emission (today `write_schemas_to_shm` writes **only** the monolith).
- The leaf+fold incremental hash (today it's `blake3` of the whole blob on **every** schema register — the O(N²)-at-boot thing we found).
- The 5→1 hash consolidation.

So: **conceptually settled, zero of it implemented, and three specifics (file format, hash plumbing, atomicity) still need your call** before I'd write code. Want to lock those three now so it's fully nailed, or leave them until we actually build the folder emission?

(Side note: the new diagnostics that just popped — `ui_gallery.rs`/`rovs_proxy.rs` unused imports/vars — are pre-existing warnings in files I didn't touch, not from this work.)

**Decisions made 2026-06-21 (Claude's judgment, user-delegated). The single producer is `op-projection::SchemaEngine::write_schemas_to_shm()`** (the schema/catalog authority; the mutation side is the renamed `MutationEngine` in op-grpc-bridge — see [[project_one_schema_single_source]]).

1. **Per-plugin file = bare `PluginSchema` object.** `/dev/shm/opdbus/schemas/<plugin>.json` IS that plugin's schema object (not the `[schema]` array the monolith map uses internally). "The schema is the plugin." Zero change to the zeroclaw bridge — it already expects the bare object. If a plugin has multiple schema docs, the file holds its canonical/primary one.

2. **Hash published via an atomic manifest, computed ONCE.** Enumerator computes per-plugin **leaf** hashes `blake3(canonical_bytes(<plugin>.json))` and folds them into one **root**: `blake3( for id in sorted(plugins): id || leaf[id] )` — incremental (a schema change re-hashes only that plugin). The root + leaves + a `generation` counter are written to `/dev/shm/opdbus/schemas/.manifest.json`. **`op-identity` (the 5 re-hash sites: schema_bridge.rs, anna_scribe.rs, op-sled-top.rs, op-identity-sled.rs, op-web/handlers/identity.rs) STOP re-reading+re-hashing `live-schema.json` and read `manifest.catalog_hash` instead.** One computation, one value.

3. **Atomicity = per-file temp+rename, manifest written LAST as the commit point.** Each `<plugin>.json` and the monolith are written temp+rename; the manifest is renamed last, so a reader sees either the whole old generation or the whole new one — never torn. Readers needing consistency consult the manifest first; `generation` detects staleness.

**`live-schema.json` survives as a DERIVED "all-together" monolith cache** (for whole-catalog readers), also temp+rename — but it is NO LONGER the hash source; the manifest root is. **Cross-boundary caveat:** swapping the identity derivation from `blake3(live-schema.json bytes)` → `manifest.catalog_hash` changes the hash VALUE, so the verifier on the other side of the WG/ghostbridge derivation must adopt the same manifest value in lockstep. Honors [[project_one_schema_single_source]]; pairs with the folder/monolith reasoning and the `source_port_salt` derivation.

**Decisions made 2026-06-21 (Claude's judgment, user-delegated). The single producer is `op-projection::SchemaEngine::write_schemas_to_shm()`** (the schema/catalog authority; the mutation side is the renamed `MutationEngine` in op-grpc-bridge — see [[project_one_schema_single_source]]).

1. **Per-plugin file = bare `PluginSchema` object.** `/dev/shm/opdbus/schemas/<plugin>.json` IS that plugin's schema object (not the `[schema]` array the monolith map uses internally). "The schema is the plugin." Zero change to the zeroclaw bridge — it already expects the bare object. If a plugin has multiple schema docs, the file holds its canonical/primary one.

2. **Hash published via an atomic manifest, computed ONCE.** Enumerator computes per-plugin **leaf** hashes `blake3(canonical_bytes(<plugin>.json))` and folds them into one **root**: `blake3( for id in sorted(plugins): id || leaf[id] )` — incremental (a schema change re-hashes only that plugin). The root + leaves + a `generation` counter are written to `/dev/shm/opdbus/schemas/.manifest.json`. **`op-identity` (the 5 re-hash sites: schema_bridge.rs, anna_scribe.rs, op-sled-top.rs, op-identity-sled.rs, op-web/handlers/identity.rs) STOP re-reading+re-hashing `live-schema.json` and read `manifest.catalog_hash` instead.** One computation, one value.

3. **Atomicity = per-file temp+rename, manifest written LAST as the commit point.** Each `<plugin>.json` and the monolith are written temp+rename; the manifest is renamed last, so a reader sees either the whole old generation or the whole new one — never torn. Readers needing consistency consult the manifest first; `generation` detects staleness.

**`live-schema.json` survives as a DERIVED "all-together" monolith cache** (for whole-catalog readers), also temp+rename — but it is NO LONGER the hash source; the manifest root is. **Cross-boundary caveat:** swapping the identity derivation from `blake3(live-schema.json bytes)` → `manifest.catalog_hash` changes the hash VALUE, so the verifier on the other side of the WG/ghostbridge derivation must adopt the same manifest value in lockstep. Honors [[project_one_schema_single_source]]; pairs with the folder/monolith reasoning and the `source_port_salt` derivation.

**Decisions made 2026-06-21 (Claude's judgment, user-delegated). The single producer is `op-projection::SchemaEngine::write_schemas_to_shm()`** (the schema/catalog authority; the mutation side is the renamed `MutationEngine` in op-grpc-bridge — see [[project_one_schema_single_source]]).

1. **Per-plugin file = bare `PluginSchema` object.** `/dev/shm/opdbus/schemas/<plugin>.json` IS that plugin's schema object (not the `[schema]` array the monolith map uses internally). "The schema is the plugin." Zero change to the zeroclaw bridge — it already expects the bare object. If a plugin has multiple schema docs, the file holds its canonical/primary one.

2. **Hash published via an atomic manifest, computed ONCE.** Enumerator computes per-plugin **leaf** hashes `blake3(canonical_bytes(<plugin>.json))` and folds them into one **root**: `blake3( for id in sorted(plugins): id || leaf[id] )` — incremental (a schema change re-hashes only that plugin). The root + leaves + a `generation` counter are written to `/dev/shm/opdbus/schemas/.manifest.json`. **`op-identity` (the 5 re-hash sites: schema_bridge.rs, anna_scribe.rs, op-sled-top.rs, op-identity-sled.rs, op-web/handlers/identity.rs) STOP re-reading+re-hashing `live-schema.json` and read `manifest.catalog_hash` instead.** One computation, one value.

3. **Atomicity = per-file temp+rename, manifest written LAST as the commit point.** Each `<plugin>.json` and the monolith are written temp+rename; the manifest is renamed last, so a reader sees either the whole old generation or the whole new one — never torn. Readers needing consistency consult the manifest first; `generation` detects staleness.

CONSUMER side PENDING — op-identity's 5 re-hash sites still `blake3(live-schema.json bytes)`; switching them to `manifest.catalog_hash` is the next pass (and needs the WG/ghostbridge verifier in lockstep).

**Decision (2026-06-21): Gemma becomes a `StatePlugin`, not an op-web handler.** The existing `crates/op-web/src/handlers/gemma.rs` is a bespoke REST shim (4 handlers: read `/dev/shm/gemma-ui-specs.json`, delete a spec, `POST regenerate` that **forks `/usr/local/bin/op-gemma`**, passthrough `/dev/shm/live-schema.json`). That is exactly the surface the schema/plugin/projection design exists to eliminate. (It's also broken WIP — `gemma.rs:36` `Path(spec_id: String) -> Path<String>)` is malformed, blocking the op-dbus build.)

**The general anti-pattern:** an op-web handler that (a) bespoke-reads a `/dev/shm` artifact or (b) forks a binary is wrong. State → a plugin's `query_current_state` published as a **projection** under `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<plugin>` (read generically, not via `/api/gemma/*`). Actions → **mutations routed through the MutationEngine** (op-grpc-bridge) so they hit the Event Chain audit + policy enforcement ("every mutation is an enforcement point"); never `tokio::process::Command` from the web tier.

**Two-plugin split (named 2026-06-21):**
- **`large-language-model`** — generic, model-AGNOSTIC inference surface. schemars config: `provider` (ollama), `model_id` (gemma3/llama/mistral…), endpoint, gen params, pull/load lifecycle. The ONLY thing that knows about Ollama. "Gemma the model" = `model_id: "gemma3"` here; nothing else hard-codes Gemma. Swappable broker stance.
- **`gemma-brain`** — umbrella COGNITIVE plugin (Gemma does multiple things, so "brain" not "router"). Owns: tag routing + subid classification (see [[project_subid_taxonomy]], [[project_xray_router]]), the 4 perspectives (see [[project_gemma_4perspectives]]), UI-spec gallery generation. CONSUMES `large-language-model` for inference — does not embed a model. "gemma" here is a brand for the brain concept, not a model binding.

Boundary: **LLM plugin = HOW to talk to a model; gemma-brain = WHAT to decide with it.** Both schemars-derived with OSCAL subids; state→projection under `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<plugin>`; actions (`regenerate`/`delete-spec`)→mutations via MutationEngine. Register in `op-plugins/src/default_registry.rs`. Then DELETE `handlers/gemma.rs` + its `/api/gemma/*` routes (also unblocks the op-dbus build). Honors [[project_one_schema_single_source]].

=== deploy/deploy.sh (build + install flow) ===
#!/bin/bash
# deploy/deploy.sh — Operation D-Bus system deployment (s6-rc)
#
# Usage:
#   sudo ./deploy/deploy.sh [--skip-network] [SERVICE|all]
#
# Services: op-dbus, op-web-server, op-chat, op-services, op-projection, op-dbus-mirror

set -euo pipefail

PROJECT_ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
DEPLOY_DIR="${PROJECT_ROOT}/deploy"
INSTALL_BIN="/usr/local/bin"
S6_SV="/etc/s6/sv"
S6_DB="/etc/s6/db"

SERVICES=(
    "op-web:op-dbus:op-dbus"
    "op-web:op-web-server:op-web-server"
    "op-chat:op-chat:chatmanager"
    "op-dbus-mirror:ovs-dbus-init:op-dbus-mirror"
    "op-projection:projection_server:op-projection"
    "op-cognitive-mcp:op-cognitive-mcp:op-cognitive-mcp"
)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Args
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

SKIP_NETWORK=false
TARGET=""

for arg in "$@"; do
    case "$arg" in
        --skip-network) SKIP_NETWORK=true ;;
        --help) echo "Usage: sudo $0 [--skip-network] [SERVICE|all]"; exit 0 ;;
        -*) echo "Unknown flag: $arg" >&2; exit 1 ;;
        *) TARGET="$arg" ;;
    esac
done

[[ "$EUID" -eq 0 ]] || { echo "Run with sudo." >&2; exit 1; }

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Logging
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

log()   { echo -e "\033[0;32m[DEPLOY]\033[0m $*"; }
warn()  { echo -e "\033[1;33m[WARN]\033[0m $*"; }
error() { echo -e "\033[0;31m[ERROR]\033[0m $*"; exit 1; }

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Helpers
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

append_env_if_missing() {
    local file="$1" key="$2" value="$3"
    grep -q "^${key}=" "$file" 2>/dev/null || printf '%s=%s\n' "$key" "$value" >> "$file"
}

s6_restart() {
    local svc="$1"
    if [[ -d "/run/service/${svc}" ]]; then
        s6-svc -r "/run/service/${svc}" && log "Restarted s6 service: ${svc}"
    else
        warn "s6 service not running: ${svc}"
    fi
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# STEP 1: System files
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

install_system_files() {
    log "Installing system files..."

    # D-Bus policy
    install -d /etc/dbus-1/system.d
    install -m 0644 "${DEPLOY_DIR}/dbus/org.opdbus.conf"  /etc/dbus-1/system.d/org.opdbus.conf
    install -m 0644 "${DEPLOY_DIR}/dbus/org.dbusmcp.conf" /etc/dbus-1/system.d/org.dbusmcp.conf

**Decisions made 2026-06-21 (Claude's judgment, user-delegated). The single producer is `op-projection::SchemaEngine::write_schemas_to_shm()`** (the schema/catalog authority; the mutation side is the renamed `MutationEngine` in op-grpc-bridge — see [[project_one_schema_single_source]]).

1. **Per-plugin file = bare `PluginSchema` object.** `/dev/shm/opdbus/schemas/<plugin>.json` IS that plugin's schema object (not the `[schema]` array the monolith map uses internally). "The schema is the plugin." Zero change to the zeroclaw bridge — it already expects the bare object. If a plugin has multiple schema docs, the file holds its canonical/primary one.

2. **Hash published via an atomic manifest, computed ONCE.** Enumerator computes per-plugin **leaf** hashes `blake3(canonical_bytes(<plugin>.json))` and folds them into one **root**: `blake3( for id in sorted(plugins): id || leaf[id] )` — incremental (a schema change re-hashes only that plugin). The root + leaves + a `generation` counter are written to `/dev/shm/opdbus/schemas/.manifest.json`. **`op-identity` (the 5 re-hash sites: schema_bridge.rs, anna_scribe.rs, op-sled-top.rs, op-identity-sled.rs, op-web/handlers/identity.rs) STOP re-reading+re-hashing `live-schema.json` and read `manifest.catalog_hash` instead.** One computation, one value.

3. **Atomicity = per-file temp+rename, manifest written LAST as the commit point.** Each `<plugin>.json` and the monolith are written temp+rename; the manifest is renamed last, so a reader sees either the whole old generation or the whole new one — never torn. Readers needing consistency consult the manifest first; `generation` detects staleness.

**Decision (2026-06-21): Gemma becomes a `StatePlugin`, not an op-web handler.** The existing `crates/op-web/src/handlers/gemma.rs` is a bespoke REST shim (4 handlers: read `/dev/shm/gemma-ui-specs.json`, delete a spec, `POST regenerate` that **forks `/usr/local/bin/op-gemma`**, passthrough `/dev/shm/live-schema.json`). That is exactly the surface the schema/plugin/projection design exists to eliminate. (It's also broken WIP — `gemma.rs:36` `Path(spec_id: String) -> Path<String>)` is malformed, blocking the op-dbus build.)

**The general anti-pattern:** an op-web handler that (a) bespoke-reads a `/dev/shm` artifact or (b) forks a binary is wrong. State → a plugin's `query_current_state` published as a **projection** under `/org/opdbus/v1/plugins/<plugin>` (read generically, not via `/api/gemma/*`). Actions → **mutations routed through the MutationEngine** (op-grpc-bridge) so they hit the Event Chain audit + policy enforcement ("every mutation is an enforcement point"); never `tokio::process::Command` from the web tier.

- **`large-language-model`** — generic, model-AGNOSTIC inference surface. schemars config: `provider` (ollama), `model_id` (gemma3/llama/mistral…), endpoint, gen params, pull/load lifecycle. The ONLY thing that knows about Ollama. "Gemma the model" = `model_id: "gemma3"` here; nothing else hard-codes Gemma. Swappable broker stance.

Owns: tag routing + subid classification (see [[project_subid_taxonomy]], [[project_xray_router]]), the 4 perspectives (see [[project_gemma_4perspectives]]), UI-spec gallery generation. CONSUMES `large-language-model` for inference — does not embed a model. "gemma" here is a brand for the brain concept, not a model binding.

content.text:
## On `anyhow`
Your instinct is right *in general* — `anyhow` in **library** code is a known smell (it erases typed errors so callers can't match on them; `thiserror` is the library-grade choice). But it's not forbidden, and **in this codebase it's the established convention**: `anyhow` appears in **396** source files vs `thiserror` in **20**, no lint/doc bans it, and critically the **`StatePlugin` trait itself returns `anyhow::Result`** — so my two plugins *must* use it to satisfy the trait. I didn't choose it; the trait dictates it. The 20 thiserror files are the lower-level crates (op-network's `OvsError`, op-state-store) that do have typed errors. Moving plugins off anyhow would mean re-typing the core trait — a workspace-wide decision, not a per-plugin one.

Yes — schema.rs is the JSON renderer. Quick map:

Inputs

schema: &schemars::Schema — Draft 2020-12 JSON Schema, produced by schemars::schema_for!(StateStruct) on plugin state types in op-plugins.
value: &serde_json::Value — live payload (typically grpc::decode_to_json(DynamicMessage) from a tonic-web stream).
Entry point

render_value(ui, schema, value) → render_node (recursive).
Per-node rendering (render_node)

Reads title, description, type from the schema; falls back to JSON path ($.foo.bar[0]) when no title.
Wraps each node in CollapsingState keyed by path, auto-open for depth < 2.
Header line: title · type, plus enum[N] badge if enum present.
Body: description in italic muted, then dispatches to render_body.
Dispatch (render_body)

Resolves oneOf / anyOf / allOf by picking the first branch (resolve_composition).
type: object → render_object
type: array → render_array
otherwise → render_leaf
Objects (render_object)

Iterates properties, recurses with path $.key.
required keys get a red ·required tag (uses DANGER theme token).
Missing values render as Null.
Arrays (render_array)

Recurses through items schema for each element with path $[i].
Shows (empty) muted italic when length 0.
Leaves (render_leaf)

Color-coded by JSON type via theme tokens:
null → MUTED (∅ null)
bool → OK / DANGER
number → PRIMARY
string → FG, quoted, monospace
Appends «format» (e.g. date-time, uuid) and default=… annotations from the schema.
Fallback

pretty_json(value) — stable pretty dump used when no schema is available (still satisfies the "no raw JSON dumps" rule because views only fall back inside a labeled diagnostic frame, e.g. gRPC Explorer raw payload view).
Where it's consumed

views::inspector — DemoPluginState schema + decoded value (live demo of the contract).
views::state_view — same pipeline for any plugin's projected state.
views::grpc_* — decodes any RPC response via reflection and renders it.

schema.rs
Yes — schema.rs is the JSON renderer. Quick map:

Inputs

schema: &schemars::Schema — Draft 2020-12 JSON Schema, produced by schemars::schema_for!(StateStruct) on plugin state types in op-plugins.
value: &serde_json::Value — live payload (typically grpc::decode_to_json(DynamicMessage) from a tonic-web stream).
Entry point

render_value(ui, schema, value) → render_node (recursive).
Per-node rendering (render_node)

Reads title, description, type from the schema; falls back to JSON path ($.foo.bar[0]) when no title.
Wraps each node in CollapsingState keyed by path, auto-open for depth < 2.
Header line: title · type, plus enum[N] badge if enum present.
Body: description in italic muted, then dispatches to render_body.
Dispatch (render_body)

Resolves oneOf / anyOf / allOf by picking the first branch (resolve_composition).
type: object → render_object
type: array → render_array
otherwise → render_leaf
Objects (render_object)

Iterates properties, recurses with path $.key.
required keys get a red ·required tag (uses DANGER theme token).
Missing values render as Null.
Arrays (render_array)

Recurses through items schema for each element with path $[i].
Shows (empty) muted italic when length 0.
Leaves (render_leaf)

Color-coded by JSON type via theme tokens:
null → MUTED (∅ null)
bool → OK / DANGER
number → PRIMARY
string → FG, quoted, monospace
Appends «format» (e.g. date-time, uuid) and default=… annotations from the schema.
Fallback

pretty_json(value) — stable pretty dump used when no schema is available (still satisfies the "no raw JSON dumps" rule because views only fall back inside a labeled diagnostic frame, e.g. gRPC Explorer raw payload view).
Where it's consumed

views::inspector — DemoPluginState schema + decoded value (live demo of the contract).
views::state_view — same pipeline for any plugin's projected state.
views::grpc_* — decodes any RPC response via reflection and renders it.

oneOf branch picker is naive (first branch); needs discriminator-aware selection for tagged unions.
$ref resolution isn't implemented — schemars 1 mostly inlines, but external refs would render as ref placeholder.

No virtualization — large arrays should switch to a windowed renderer before we point this at log-shaped payloads.

Thought for 21s
Honest take first — three of the four choices are right, one needs a guardrail before it ships.

Right calls

gRPC stream from gemma over the existing tonic-web channel. Matches the rest of the system (reflection-based, projection-shaped, WireGuard-fronted). Pulling from json-render.dev at runtime would have broken the air-gap posture.
Declarative DSL → single egui interpreter (over WASM-per-element). WASM-per-element would mean a sandbox cost per widget, a cold-start per mint, and a much larger attack surface. One interpreter is auditable and fast.
Catalog as authoritative, no raw-JSON fallback. Without that, the old ad-hoc renderers crawl back in within a week.
The one I'd push back on: "rolling 200, mint-on-use/retire, novel options humans wouldn't think of." Two real risks for an operator console:

Churn breaks bindings. A view bound to element_id=X becomes a hard error the moment gemma retires X. For an ops console where muscle memory matters (you'll be staring at the Services view at 3am), surprise widget swaps are hostile.
Novelty fights operability. "Options a human wouldn't think of" is great for a gallery, dangerous for a control surface where misclicking restarts s6 services.
I'd add two guardrails without changing the spirit:

Versioned, immutable element IDs. Retirement removes from the active gallery, not from the resolver. Views keep working on a pinned element_id@version until an operator explicitly accepts a migration.
A "stable core" subset inside the 200 (say 40 elements) that gemma may not retire — reserved for primitives operators rely on (button, toggle, select, numeric input, table row, status pill, log line, form field). The other ~160 slots are gemma's novelty playground.
I'll bake both into the scaffolding so they don't have to be retrofitted.

Thought for 28s
Right — you're after interaction primitives for dense data and gesture-first nav. Concrete catalog seeds gemma can riff on:

Crawling huge trees

Miller columns (Finder-style cascading panes) — each level scrolls independently; never lose your place in a 100k-node tree.
Fisheye / focus+context lens — current row at full size, siblings shrink with distance. Pad / Sheelagh Carpendale's classic.
Treemap with semantic zoom — rectangles sized by metric (log volume, error count, bytes); click to descend, breadcrumbs to ascend.
Icicle / sunburst — hierarchical flame layout; great for "where is the weight."
Indented tree with sparkline gutters — every row carries a tiny inline chart of its subtree's recent activity. Spot anomalies without expanding.
Hyperbolic tree — root in center, depth bends toward the edge; thousands of nodes on one screen, drag to reframe.
Cone tree / 3D radial — overkill for most things but stunning for very wide branching.
Frozen-path crumbtrail — pinned ancestor chain at the top that stays interactive while you wander the subtree.
Quickfilter-as-you-type with structural preservation — non-matching nodes collapse to thin bars instead of disappearing, so the shape of the tree is preserved.
Differential tree — two trees overlaid with red/green diff markers per node, for "what changed since last poll."
Mouseover / gesture nav

Marking menus (Kurtenbach) — radial menus that learn your muscle memory; experts flick directions without looking, novices wait for the pie to appear. Hugely underused.
Hover-trails — moving the cursor along a path triggers nav (vs clicking). Think Mission Control corners but inside the app.
Pressure / dwell rings — hover with intent indicator filling up before commit; safer than instant hover-fire.
Spatially persistent panels — panels live at fixed screen regions; hover-to-peek, click-to-pin. Operator builds muscle memory by location.
Lens cursor — area around cursor renders at higher detail or with extra metadata overlay (timestamps, ids, raw values).
Predictive prefetch on hover-vector — direction + velocity of mouse predicts which panel to warm up; feels instant.
Edge-gesture drawers — flick toward a screen edge to summon that edge's drawer; release to pin.
Bezel / off-canvas peek — pull data in from outside the viewport without leaving the current view.
Hover-scrub timeline — single horizontal strip; hover any pixel = preview that moment's full state in a ghosted overlay.
Dense data interaction (worth including)

Brush + link — drag-select on one chart highlights matching rows everywhere else on screen. Foundational, still rare in ops tools.
Sparkline grids with hover-detail-on-demand.
Heatmap calendar (GitHub-style) for any time-bucketed metric.
Horizon charts — band-folded line charts; 10× density vs a normal line.
Bullet graphs (Stephen Few) — replaces gauges; quantitative + qualitative + target in one row.
Punchcard (day × hour) — instant visual pattern of when things happen.
Confirm / commit / undo (the part that matters at 3am)

Drag-to-confirm for destructive ops — drag a knob across a gap; cancellable mid-drag.
Hold-to-fire with progress ring, releasing aborts.
Two-finger / two-key chord commit — physical interlock.
Reversible toast — action fires immediately, toast holds for N seconds with undo; commit silently after.
Shadow-state preview — toggling a switch shows the would-be state ghosted before you commit.
Uncertainty / liveness (operator-specific)

Staleness halo — every value carries a soft ring whose opacity decays with age since last update.
Confidence whiskers on numbers — ±error bars inline next to the value.
Heartbeat dots — tiny pulsing dot per source; missed beats go red without alarm fatigue.
Provenance hover — hover any value, get the source RPC + timestamp + decoder path as a floating chip.
Worth feeding gemma as prior art to surpass, not to clone. Want me to drop these into mem://features/generative-ui/inspiration-primitives as a reference file so gemma's prompt can pull them when minting?

how can i suggest those things to gemma without naming them, because as soon as a suggestion has a name, it has a "pattern" and is now normalized and not a random thing a human wouldnt think of.


Thought for 25s
Sharp instinct. The moment you write "marking menu" she'll generate marking menus. The trick is to strip every word that has a Wikipedia page and feed her only the forces the design has to resolve. Pattern names are compressed solutions — give her the uncompressed problem instead.

A few techniques that work:

1. Describe the problem in physics, not UI. Bad: "fisheye lens for trees." Good: "The operator needs to read one row in full detail while staying aware of 200 rows above and below it. Screen real estate is fixed. Scrolling loses context. The far rows matter less than near rows but must not vanish."

She'll invent her own resolution. It might be a fisheye, or it might be something nobody has named yet.

2. Specify constraints and forbid solutions, not name them. "No modal. No new page. No scrollbar. Operator's hand never leaves the home row. Decision must be reversible for 3 seconds. Destructive action must require two distinct physical inputs." Constraints generate; names imitate.

3. Describe the sensation/intent, not the mechanism. "Feel: peeking around a corner without committing to walk through the door." "Feel: a held breath — input received, not yet executed." "Feel: the value is fresh, but how fresh?" "Feel: I changed my mind, and the system already knew."

4. Give her the failure mode she's avoiding. "At 3am, the operator will misclick. Design so that the worst misclick costs nothing." "The operator has been staring at this for 6 hours. Yes — schema.rs is the JSON renderer. Quick map:

Inputs

schema: &schemars::Schema — Draft 2020-12 JSON Schema, produced by schemars::schema_for!(StateStruct) on plugin state types in op-plugins.
value: &serde_json::Value — live payload (typically grpc::decode_to_json(DynamicMessage) from a tonic-web stream).
Entry point

render_value(ui, schema, value) → render_node (recursive).
Per-node rendering (render_node)

Reads title, description, type from the schema; falls back to JSON path ($.foo.bar[0]) when no title.
Wraps each node in CollapsingState keyed by path, auto-open for depth < 2.
Header line: title · type, plus enum[N] badge if enum present.
Body: description in italic muted, then dispatches to render_body.
Dispatch (render_body)

Resolves oneOf / anyOf / allOf by picking the first branch (resolve_composition).
type: object → render_object
type: array → render_array
otherwise → render_leaf
Objects (render_object)

Iterates properties, recurses with path $.key.
required keys get a red ·required tag (uses DANGER theme token).
Missing values render as Null.
Arrays (render_array)

Recurses through items schema for each element with path $[i].
Shows (empty) muted italic when length 0.
Leaves (render_leaf)

Color-coded by JSON type via theme tokens:
null → MUTED (∅ null)
bool → OK / DANGER
number → PRIMARY
string → FG, quoted, monospace
Appends «format» (e.g. date-time, uuid) and default=… annotations from the schema.
Fallback

pretty_json(value) — stable pretty dump used when no schema is available (still satisfies the "no raw JSON dumps" rule because views only fall back inside a labeled diagnostic frame, e.g. gRPC Explorer raw payload view).

views::inspector — DemoPluginState schema + decoded value (live demo of the contract).

content.text:
Here's the backend ownership map I was enforcing this session — each authority lives in exactly one place, with a hard boundary on what it does *not* own:

## Schema vs Mutation — the two engines (the core split)
- **`op-projection::SchemaEngine` = schema/catalog authority.** Sole producer of the SHM catalog: `write_schemas_to_shm()` writes the per-plugin folder + `live-schema.json` cache + `.manifest.json` with the **one** `catalog_hash`. *Does not* route mutations or touch the sled.
- **`op-grpc-bridge::MutationEngine` = mutation authority.** Routes all mutations (gRPC + D-Bus), records the Event Chain, owns the Identity Sled `mutation_index`. *Does not* own the schema catalog.
- They line up 1:1 with the identity derivation terms: `Blake3(wg_pubkey ‖ schema_catalog_hash ‖ mutation_index ‖ source_port)` — schema engine owns the first, mutation engine the second.

## Single source of truth
- **The catalog is written in one place** (op-projection's enumerator) — no competing writer.
- **The `catalog_hash` is computed once** — op-identity's 5 re-hash sites collapsed to one `schema_bridge::schema_catalog_hash()`. Everyone else **reads** it; nobody re-derives.

## Plugins
- **Each plugin owns its own schema** (schemars-derived, schema-is-the-plugin). No aggregate `schema_def` authority.
- Plugins are **declarative**: they own `schema()` + `query_current_state()`. They **do not** own mutation execution (that's the MutationEngine; `apply_state` is a no-op by convention) and **do not** self-write SHM (the enumerator publishes).

## The tree
- **`/org/opdbus/v1/plugins` is the only D-Bus tree.** No service or object path outside it — which is why I rejected a standalone `CatalogService`. The catalog is a **`gemma_brain` projection** under `/plugins/gemma_brain`, not a bespoke service.

## op-web
- **Transport only** — thin API/gRPC surface. Handlers that read SHM bespoke or fork binaries don't belong here; they become plugins/projections/mutations. Stripped the SPA-serving entirely (op-web is API/gRPC, the React SPA is not the runtime).

## Gemma split
- **`large_language_model` = the *how*** — generic, model-agnostic inference surface; the only Ollama-aware thing; model is a swappable field.
- **`gemma_brain` = the *what*** — cognitive decisions (routing/classification/perspectives) + catalog ownership; consumes the LLM plugin, embeds no model.

## Deferred (recorded, not enforced yet)
- **zeroclaw** should become the single **LLM provider/model routing** authority (consolidating `op-llm`'s runtime switching) — OD-28.

The through-line: **one producer per fact, consumers only read, one tree, declarative plugins, transport stays dumb.**

content.text:
Everything works exactly as designed. Here's the live verification:

- **`PluginService.ListPlugins`** → `Unauthenticated: A.N.N.A. Scribe: Missing Ghostbridge Identity Sled` — this is the **correct** result. It proves PluginService is mounted *and* the `GhostbridgeInterceptor` (Zero Trust / Absolute Base gate) is active. My host-side `grpcurl` carries no identity sled, so it's dropped; a real container connects with its xraqy/WG-injected sled and passes.
- **`ZeroclawService.GetSchema`** → returns the live schema (discovery surface, ungated).
- Bridge log shows it up and serving (the WARN lines are just the trace layer stamping sentinel footprints for my unauthenticated probes).

## What was wrong and what I fixed

The assistant container — like every container — connects to the one shared `container.sock` bridge, which runs `run_zeroclaw_server` (`server.rs`). That function mounted **only** `ZeroclawService` + `PluginService`. Reflection, `ChatService`, and `DbusPassthrough` had all been added to `run_grpc_server` in `grpc_server.rs` — **a different binary** — so `grpcurl :8090 list` returned *"server does not support the reflection API,"* contradicting `chat_service.rs`'s own claim that zeroclaw-gui discovers it "via a single reflection endpoint."

Fix (`crates/op-grpc-bridge/src/server.rs`): consolidated the bridge's service surface into one `build_routes()` used by both the UDS and TCP listeners, now mounting:

| Service | Purpose for the assistant container |
|---|---|
| `gRPC reflection` (v1) | zeroclaw-gui discovers every service from this one endpoint |
| `ChatService` | the operator chat stream it's meant to find |
| `DbusPassthrough` | generic D-Bus call/get/set — the `ai.assistant.v1` extension path |
| `PluginService` | `createunixsocket` via `CallMethod` → unix-socket plugin |
| `ZeroclawService` | schema get/watch |

The assistant is provisioned **the same as other containers**: its socket is created via the unix-socket plugin's `createsocket` (`CallMethod` → `UnixSocketPlugin::create_unix_socket`), not a raw Incus proxy device, and all of this is identity-gated by the interceptor.

## Status
- Built clean (lib + bin + tests, exit 0; only pre-existing warnings).
- Test `zeroclaw_integration.rs` updated for the new `build_axum_app` signature.
- Release binary installed to `/usr/local/bin/op-grpc-bridge-zeroclaw`, service restarted (PID 7003), reflection confirmed live on `:8090`.

Two notes, no action taken:
1. Reflection lists all descriptor services (StateSync, Mail, etc.); only the four above are actually mounted — calling the rest returns `Unimplemented`. Cosmetic; the assistant-relevant ones are all live.
2. `ChatService.Send` is still the deferred stub (echoes; `TODO: wire to gemma_brain`) — that's **OD-28** (zeroclaw owns LLM routing), which you said to deal with later. Discovery/transport is fixed; the pipeline behind it is the deferred piece.

Changes are deployed but **not committed**. Want me to commit them to `feat/sled-source-port-salt`?

- skills: Reference codebase for Crates. Use this skill when you need to understand the structure, implementation patterns, or code details of the Crates project.
- mcp-server-dev:build-mcp-app: This skill should be used when the user wants to build an "MCP app", add "interactive UI" or "widgets" to an MCP server, "render components in chat", build "MCP UI resources", make a tool that shows a "form", "picker", "dashboard" or "confirmation dialog" inline in the conversation, or mentions "apps SDK" in the context of MCP. Use AFTER the build-mcp-server skill has settled the deployment model, or when the user already knows they want UI widgets.
- mcp-server-dev:build-mcp-server: This skill should be used when the user asks to "build an MCP server", "create an MCP", "make an MCP integration", "wrap an API for Claude", "expose tools to Claude", "make an MCP app", or discusses building something with the Model Context Protocol. It is the entry point for MCP server development — it interrogates the user about their use case, determines the right deployment model (remote HTTP, MCPB, local stdio), picks a tool-design pattern, and hands off to specialized skills.
- mcp-server-dev:build-mcpb: This skill should be used when the user wants to "package an MCP server", "bundle an MCP", "make an MCPB", "ship a local MCP server", "distribute a local MCP", discusses ".mcpb files", mentions bundling a Node or Python runtime with their MCP server, or needs an MCP server that interacts with the local filesystem, desktop apps, or OS and must be installable without the user having Node/Python set up.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- verify: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by running the app and observing behavior. Use when asked to verify a PR, confirm a fix works, test a change manually, check that a feature works, or validate local changes before pushing.
- code-review: Review the current diff for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud). Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
